newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to decide on religious freedom law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to decide on religious freedom law.

text.p: The Supreme Court said Tuesday it would hear a constitutional challenge to a 1993 federal law that establishes greater protection for the exercise of religion in the face of government regulation.
The justices agreed to review a U.S. appeals court ruling that upheld as constitutional the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The ruling overturned a federal judge's decision striking down the law.

Under the law, federal, state and local government agencies must accommodate a religious practice unless the government can prove it has a compelling interest in regulating it and the regulation chosen was the least restrictive means possible.

The law had been challenged on the grounds that Congress had overstepped its authority in adopting it and that it violated the First Amendment by giving religion exclusive privileges over other expressions of conscience.
The justices will hear arguments in the case early next year, with a decision due by the end of the court term in June.
The case arose after Boerne, Texas, denied an application from a Roman Catholic archbishop for a permit to expand a church because it was within the city's historic district.
Citing a large increase in parishioners, the church said it would be unable to accomplish its mission and survive as a parish church unless it expanded.
The archbishop sued, claiming the denial of the construction permit violated the 1993 law. The city replied that the law was unconstitutional.

After losing at the appeals court, the city asked the Supreme Court to hold that the law improperly requires state and local governments to accommodate religious exercise to a greater extent than the Constitution requires. Several states supported the appeal.
The Justice Department, backed by a number of religious groups, defended the law and said further review of the case was unwarranted.
